strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies the semantic-acoustic trade-off in existing codecs and proposes an intuitive dual-stream solution

Strong empirical results: achieves state-of-the-art or near-SOTA across reconstruction metrics (UTMOS, WER, PESQ) and semantic representation (ARCH benchmark), demonstrating both reconstruction quality and semantic fidelity
Comprehensive evaluation: rigorous assessment across multiple bitrates, clean and noisy conditions, with extensive baseline comparisons and ablation studies

Insightful disentanglement analysis: Section 5.4 convincingly demonstrates clean semantic-acoustic separation through semantic-only/acoustic-only reconstruction and mel-spectrogram visualization; SAC achieves WER of 3.99 in semantic-only mode vs. 30.67 for SemantiCodec
Practical utility: semantic representation competitive with some SSL models (outperforms wav2vec 2.0, data2vec); supports multiple bitrates; robustness under noisy conditions
Good reproducibility: detailed training setup, hyperparameters in appendices, promise to release code/models; comprehensive data statistics provided
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing components (frozen pre-trained tokenizer, Encodec architecture, standard VQ-GAN) without deep methodological innovation; the dual-stream combination, while effective, is relatively incremental

Strong dependency on external semantic tokenizer: semantic stream is frozen and entirely dependent on Zeng et al. (2024b); no end-to-end training; performance bounded by external component; limits generalizability to new languages/domains

Insufficient architectural ablations: Table 4 only ablates supervision terms; missing ablations on freezing vs. fine-tuning semantic stream, fusion point selection, ConvNeXt prenet alternatives, and justification for frame rate choices (25 Hz vs. 50 Hz)

Incomplete main-table comparisons: SemantiCodec (key baseline for semantic-acoustic decoupling) absent from Tables 1-2; only appears in Table 3 and Appendix D, limiting direct reconstruction comparison

Representation evaluation constraints: ARCH relies on simple time-pooling + linear probing (acknowledged limitation on p. 7) that may not reveal fine-grained differences; no downstream task evaluation (TTS, speech understanding, dialogue) despite mentioning these applications
Statistical rigor concerns: no error bars or significance tests; some improvements modest (e.g., WER 2.35% vs. 2.46%); unclear which differences are meaningful
Hyperparameter transparency: loss coefficients appear large (λ_sem=1000, λ_spk=10) without justification or sensitivity analysis; unclear how these values were selected

Generalization limitations: approach is fundamentally speech-specific with ASR-supervised semantic tokenizer; no evaluation on other languages beyond Chinese/English; cannot extend to music/general audio (acknowledged but unaddressed)
Computational efficiency not discussed: only parameter counts provided; no inference speed, latency, or memory comparison with baselines; missing analysis of computational complexity
Potential data leakage: LibriSpeech appears in both training data and evaluation; paper mentions 'official training splits' but doesn't explicitly confirm test set disjointness

UTMOS > ground truth anomaly: SAC achieves higher UTMOS than ground truth on test-other (3.84 vs. 3.50); explanation that decoder acts as generator is concerning for a codec and suggests possible artifacts rather than fidelity

Marginal speaker supervision effects: Table 4 shows removing L_spk degrades SIM significantly (0.78→0.65) but minimally affects other metrics; suggests this component may be non-essential to core framework

strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing genuine limitations of fusion-based semantic-acoustic codecs
Elegant dual-stream architecture with principled design: frozen semantic tokenizer preserves linguistic content while separate acoustic stream handles fine-grained details
Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation: reconstruction metrics, semantic representation, cross-bitrate performance, noisy conditions, and ablations
Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art WER (2.35%, near ground truth 2.16%), competitive semantic representation with SSL models, consistent performance across bitrates
Exceptional disentanglement analysis with compelling quantitative and visual evidence (semantic-only WER: 3.99 vs SemantiCodec: 30.67; SIM 0.17 showing clean speaker separation)
Practical applications identified (speaker anonymization, voice conversion, controllable TTS)
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, dataset composition, training procedures; promise to release code
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing components (frozen pre-trained tokenizer, Encodec-style acoustic encoder, standard ERes2Net speaker supervision) rather than proposing new methods
Strong dependence on pre-trained semantic tokenizer quality with limited exploration of sensitivity to tokenizer choice or impact of suboptimal tokenizers
UTMOS score exceeds ground truth (4.25 vs 4.09) which is counterintuitive and unexplained—raises concerns about overfitting to perceptual metrics or evaluation artifacts

Limited downstream evaluation: semantic representation only assessed via ARCH linear probing with global pooling; no actual downstream task results (TTS quality, speech understanding); paper acknowledges need for more fine-grained tasks
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or cross-dataset evaluation; some baseline results cited from original papers rather than reproduced
Semantic supervision (Lsem) ablation in Table 4 shows minimal impact despite being presented as important, suggesting potential redundancy with frozen semantic stream
Generalization limitations: semantic tokenizer relies on ASR supervision (limits non-speech audio); trained only on Chinese-English bilingual data; not evaluated on cross-lingual or non-speech tasks

Missing analyses: no information-theoretic characterization of what each stream encodes, no quantification of redundancy between streams, limited discussion of semantic-reconstruction quality trade-offs
Comparison fairness concerns: some TS3-Codec results taken from original paper (not reproduced); different codebook sizes and training data across baselines complicate direct comparison

strengths: Technically sound dual-stream architecture that effectively addresses the semantic-acoustic trade-off in speech codecs through principled design (frozen semantic stream, independent acoustic modeling)

Comprehensive evaluation across reconstruction, semantic representation, downstream TTS, and disentanglement dimensions with 15+ baselines, multiple bitrates, clean/noisy conditions, ablations, and subjective MOS
Strong empirical results: SOTA reconstruction (UTMOS 4.25), semantic representation (57.57% on ARCH), and TTS performance (0.90% CER on Chinese), demonstrating practical value

Remarkable disentanglement properties demonstrated rigorously: semantic-only reconstruction preserves intelligibility (3.99% WER) while removing speaker identity (MSIM 0.64), enabling controllable speech generation
Excellent reproducibility: detailed training setup, data composition, loss coefficients, efficiency analysis (RTF 0.0135), and promised code/model release
Robust performance across challenging conditions: maintains quality under noise (Tables 7-8), generalizes to low-resource settings (Table 11), and achieves superior real-time efficiency (Table 12)
weaknesses: Limited relevance to ACL's core scope: despite value for speech-LLMs, this is primarily a speech codec (audio signal processing) contribution rather than an NLP contribution; better suited for ICASSP/Interspeech, suggesting Findings rather than Main Conference track

Incremental novelty: combines existing components (frozen semantic tokenizer + acoustic codec + auxiliary losses) without introducing fundamentally new concepts; distinction from SemantiCodec could be clearer

Narrow generalization testing: evaluation uses only one semantic tokenizer (Zeng et al., 2024b); generalization to other semantic tokenizers (HuBERT-based, etc.) and audio domains (music, sound) remains unexplored

Practical limitations inadequately addressed: speaker similarity drops significantly in TTS (0.54 vs 0.58-0.67 for baselines) due to low token rate (37.5 Hz), and freezing semantic stream prevents task-specific adaptation
Limited downstream evaluation scope: primarily focuses on TTS; evaluation on ASR, speaker verification, or other speech tasks would strengthen claims of broad utility
Small-scale subjective evaluation: MOS study uses 30 utterances with 20 raters versus typical 50-100; author-reproduced baselines may introduce implementation-dependent confounds

Auxiliary feature supervision complexity inadequately justified: semantic and speaker supervision contribute <1% to results (Table 13), questioning whether added pipeline complexity (pre-extracting Sc, Sp) is warranted
